classical

Cic. ND 2.95: quī sub terrā semper habitāvissent

sub

preposition: with the ablative for where a thing is, with the accusative for where it goes

under, beneath

The ablative for rest, sub tēctō, under a roof; the accusative for motion, sub orbem sōlis, passing beneath the sun’s disc. Of a hill or a wall, at its foot: sub monte cōnsēdit (Caes. BG 1.48, Lewis & Short). For “below”, lower than, see below (īnfrā, subter).

Examples

  • quantō est facilius mihi sub tēctō vīvere

    how much easier it is for me to live under a roofPhaedr. 3.7.17

  • saepe exiguus mūs sub terrīs posuitque domōs atque horrea fēcit

    often the tiny mouse has made his home and built his barns beneath the groundVerg. G. 1.181–182

  • manet sub Jove frīgidō vēnātor

    the hunter stays out under the cold skyHor. C. 1.1.25–26

  • certō illud tempore fierī et necessāriō, cum tōta sē lūna sub orbem sōlis subjēcisset

    that this happens at a fixed time and of necessity, when the whole moon has passed beneath the sun’s discCic. Rep. 1.25

See also above, below, build.
